full_judgment:
2. Facts of the case, briefly, are, that appellants along with others were retrenched by respondent No. 2 with effect from 1-11-1980 due to temporary close down of the factory and as per a prior agreement between the Employees'' Union of the Establishment and respondent No. 2, the management was obliged to reemploy the retrenched workers as and when the factory re-started functioning. The factory reopened in January 1981 but respondent No. 2 re-employed only some junior workers ignoring the senior workers whereupon the Employees'' Union filed IRO Case No. 46 of 1981 in the First Labour Court, Dhaka under section 34 of the Industrial. Relations Ordinance and upon a contested hearing the Labour Court by its order dated 17-5-82 directed respondent No. 2 to re-employ the workers as per list in the plaint within 30 days from date. The appellants alleged that respondent No. 2 instead of re-employing them as directed by the Labour Court filed revision petition before the Zonal Martial Law Administrator against the order of the Labour Court. The appellants filed criminal case against respondent No. 2 in the First Labour Court for non-compliance of the Court''s order which was still pending. The Zonal Martial Law Administrator did not take any action on the revision petition filed by respondent No. 2 and ultimately returned the case to the First Labour Court for disposal. Respondent No. 2 then offered to re-employ the appellants by letter dated 2-11-84 whereupon they joined their service with effect from 25-11-84 but within 22 days i.e., on 18 December, 1984 respondent No. 2 terminated their service offering them all termination benefits under section 19 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 (hereinafter called the Act). 

 3. The appellants challenged the orders of termination by filing complaint case No. 18, 26, 25 and 20 of 1985 respectively under section 25(1) (b) of the Act on the ground, inter alia, of mala fide and victimization for their trade union activities. Respondent No. 2 contested the cases denying the allegations of the appellants and asserting that their services were lawfully terminated. 

 4. The Labour Court by its judgment and order dated 11 November 1986 dismissed the complaint cases holding, inter alia, that the appellants could not prove that their services were terminated by way of victimization for their trade union activities as alleged. 

 6. It was submitted while praying for leave to appeal that on the admitted facts and in the face of the record the termination of the appellants from service was out and out mala fide, that it was a case of dismissal in the garb of termination and further that it was a case of victimization for trade union activities. 

 7. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate-on-Record for the appellants, developed the aforesaid submission at the hearing of the appeals. He contended that the malafide of respondent No. 2 would be apparent in that he did not comply with to judgment and order of the Labour Court dated 17-5-82 passed in IRO Case No. 46 of 1981 directing him to re-employ the appellants within 30 days from date and instead filed a revision petition to the Zonal Martial Law Administrator to frustrate the order of the Labour Court. Ultimately, however, Respondent No. 2 made a show of employment by taking in the appellants for about 3 weeks and then terminated their service by order dated 18-12-84 which clearly shows that the respondent was never serious in re-employing the appellants either under the agreement dated 3-10-80 or in terms of the direction of the Labour Court dated 17-5-82. Mr. Chaklader submitted that the appellants were admittedly office-bearers of the Employees'' Union of the Establishment and it is, therefore, apparent that respondent No. 2 victimized them for their trade union activities taking recourse to the provision of termination which was an abuse of the said provision. 

 9. As for the grievance that the direction of the Labour Court dated 17-5-82 given in IRO Case No. 64 of 1981 to re-employ the appellants within 30 days was not complied with, it is found that respondent No. 2 filed revision petition No. 87 of 1983 before the Zonal Martial Law Administrator, Zone-A under article 2 of the Martial Law Order No. 19 of 1982 against the judgment and order of the Labour Court and the matter remained pending there. Following repeal on MLO No. 19 of 1982 as per decision contained in CMLA''s secretariat letter No. 6501/3/Labour/ML-2 dated 13-6-84 the record of the revision case was returned to the Labour Court whereupon respondent No. 2 without any delay offered to re-employ the appellants and they were, in fact, re-employed on 25-11-84. 

 10. The Labour Court upon considering the aforesaid facts therefore found no illegality in the order of reemployment passed by respondent No. 2 after the revision case had abated before the ZMLA. 

 13. It appears that at the time of hearing of the leave petition an affidavit was filed on behalf of respondent No. 2 at our direction in which it was stated that the appellants were paid their termination benefits in full. There has been no grievance made before us that the appellants have been deprived of any part of the benefits which they were entitled to upon their re-employment on 25-11-84 and on their termination of service from 18-12-84. In the circumstances of the case, we do not think that there has been any miscarriage of justice calling for interferences by this Court.
